Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of the page found by search. The default scaffold uses an in-memory SQLite database, so catalog data is lost on restart (use database.client pg outside development); unpinned plugins break after a core upgrade (check versions, upgrade on a cadence); secrets belong in environment variable substitution from Kubernetes Secrets or a secrets manager, never committed in app-config.

Found by search 2026-11-17 and read only through the search listing (title and address); to verify against the page. Used for: day-two operation of the catalog: ingestion, refresh and troubleshooting.

The company, the repositories, the services and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the platform engineer at Brindle Health, a fictional clinic network. A team stood up Backstage from the scaffold last month and pointed 300 developers at it. This morning every catalog entry disappeared after a node restart, and a security scan found a GitHub token in the repository.
handover: The deployment: one backend pod behind an ingress, database.client better-sqlite3 with connection ':memory:'.
app-config.production.yaml holds the GitHub integration token in plain text.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the map shows each component and its status in words.
Move on a check-in at a time. A decision comes to you at each check-in; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Check-in 2: the pod restarts again on a deploy; the catalog is empty for 40 minutes and the scaffolder's task history is gone.
Check-in 3: a contractor's laptop with a clone is stolen; the token is used to read private repositories before anyone revokes it.
Check-in 4: a network scan finds the portal on plain HTTP; session tokens were visible on the clinic network.

else.log: The portal is back for the afternoon.

effects.log: Check-in 1: developers are asking where the catalog went.
Check-in 2: the security team wants the token handled today.
Check-in 3: the portal went down again during a node drain.

dbPrompt.title: The catalog is in memory
dbPrompt.context: The scaffold's default is in-memory SQLite. The clinic's infrastructure team runs a managed PostgreSQL service.

choices.label: Configure database.client pg in app-config.production.yaml against the managed PostgreSQL, with credentials from environment variables, and let the catalog re-ingest once

effects.log: The backend now uses PostgreSQL; the catalog re-ingests and stays.

choices.feedback: PostgreSQL is the production database for Backstage; the catalog and the scaffolder's state persist.

choices.label: Keep SQLite but write it to a file on a persistent volume

effects.log: SQLite now writes to a volume.

choices.feedback: It survives restarts, but ties the backend to one pod and one volume; it will not scale or fail over.

choices.label: Keep it in memory and add a startup script that re-registers every location

effects.log: A startup script re-registers locations on each start.

choices.feedback: Each restart still wipes the catalog; manual registrations and the scaffolder's history are lost every time.

secretPrompt.title: A token committed in the config
secretPrompt.context: The GitHub token is in app-config.production.yaml and the repository's history.

choices.label: Revoke and rotate the token, replace it with an environment variable reference (GITHUB_TOKEN) in the config, and inject it from a Kubernetes Secret

effects.log: The old token is revoked; the new one comes from a Secret at runtime.

choices.feedback: A committed secret is compromised: rotate it, and let the config read it from the environment.

choices.label: Move the token into a ConfigMap and delete it from the YAML in a new commit

effects.log: The token moves to a ConfigMap; the old commit still has it.

choices.feedback: It is still in Git history and unrotated, and a ConfigMap is not a place for secrets.

choices.label: Leave it; the repository is private

effects.log: The token stays in the repository.

choices.feedback: Everyone with read access to the repository can use the token, and a private repository can be cloned anywhere.

haPrompt.title: One pod, no probes
haPrompt.context: One backend pod with no readiness or liveness probes; a node drain took the portal down for six minutes. Now on PostgreSQL, the backend can run several replicas.

choices.label: Run two or more replicas with readiness and liveness probes on the backend's health endpoints, a PodDisruptionBudget, and TLS at the ingress

effects.log: Two replicas with probes and a PDB serve behind the ingress.

choices.feedback: With state in PostgreSQL, replicas and health probes let the ingress route only to ready pods through drains.

choices.label: Add probes but keep one replica

effects.log: Probes are added to the single pod.

choices.feedback: Probes help the ingress, but a single pod still goes down on every drain.

choices.label: Bypass the ingress with a NodePort on plain HTTP so drains are someone else's problem

effects.log: The backend is exposed on a NodePort over HTTP.

choices.feedback: Sign-in tokens now cross the network unencrypted, and the backend is reachable without the ingress's controls.

reflection.question: Write the change record: why the catalog vanished, how the token was handled, and how the portal now stays up.

scoring.modelReasoning: The scaffold's in-memory SQLite is a development default: production Backstage uses PostgreSQL so the catalog and scaffolder state survive restarts and the backend can run replicas. Configuration layers app-config.production.yaml over the base, and secrets enter through environment substitution from a secret store; a committed secret must be revoked and rotated, not just moved. Behind an ingress with TLS, replicas with readiness and liveness probes on the health endpoints and a PodDisruptionBudget keep it up through node drains.
